subtitulo: Massacres, two civil wars, and an independence decided by three foreign fleets (1821 – 1832)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for

items.text: In Athens, the National Historical Museum, in the old Parliament building on Kolokotroni Square, is where the story of the revolution is told officially: weapons, flags, portraits of the chiefs, Byron's helmet. Go with the question of what is shown and what is missing. Look for whether Tripoli appears. Look for whether the civil wars appear. The absence is as informative as the presence, and comparing it to the Museo de la Nación or the Lugar de la Memoria in Lima is an exercise in the sociology of memory you can carry out in a single afternoon.

Facing today's Parliament, in Syntagma Square, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and the changing of the Evzones guard, in their fustanella uniform — the pleated kilt that was the dress of the irregular fighters of 1821, that is, the clothing of mountain bandits turned into the state's ceremonial uniform. It is a remarkable synthesis: the modern state dresses itself in the clothes of the men it had to subdue in order to exist.

In Corfu, remember that the island did not take part as territory: it was under the British flag, and the protectorate administration actively suppressed material support for the insurgents, though many Corfiots gave it anyway. The island was a refuge, not a front. When we reach the 1864 cession in the next entrega, that initial distance will explain why the incorporation of the Ionian Islands into the Greek kingdom was negotiated in London rather than conquered from Athens.

sections.heading: Starting with what the national holiday leaves out
paragraphs: The Greek revolution is commemorated on March 25 with school parades, flags, and the scene — constructed after the fact — of the bishop blessing the standard. What follows is an attempt to reconstruct what actually happened, which is considerably darker and considerably more instructive.

In September 1821, the insurgents took Tripoli, the Ottoman administrative capital of the Peloponnese, and massacred its Muslim and Jewish population. Estimates of the dead range from several thousand to more than ten thousand, most of them civilians, over the course of several days. In April 1822, the Ottoman reprisal on the island of Chios — which had not started the revolt, but had been dragged into it by an expedition from Samos — produced a massacre and a mass deportation: of a population in the tens of thousands, only a few thousand remained, the rest dead or sold as slaves in the markets of Anatolia. Delacroix painted Chios and Europe was moved; no one painted Tripoli.

This symmetry is drawn here not to establish moral equivalence — power imbalances matter, and the empire had means the insurgents did not — but to fix a structural finding: THE WAR OF INDEPENDENCE WAS ALSO A WAR OF RECIPROCAL RELIGIOUS CLEANSING in a territory where communities had long been intermixed. The Muslim population of the Peloponnese, present for centuries, all but vanished between 1821 and 1830. That is the material outcome of the principle we examined in entrega 13: if the nation is defined by lineage and religion, the prior mixture becomes the problem to be eliminated. In 1821 Greece inaugurates a procedure the Balkans would repeat throughout the twentieth century, and which would culminate in 1923.

sections.heading: The two civil wars of 1824 and 1825
paragraphs: Three years into the revolution, it paused to fight itself. The factions corresponded to precise social interests, which is why the episode is so sociologically legible. On one side, the MILITARY CHIEFS of the Peloponnese, led by Theodoros Kolokotronis, men of the armed bands from entrega 10, whose capital was their personal troops. On another, the landed NOTABLES of the provinces, accustomed to administering the tax collection under the Ottomans and determined to inherit the state. On a third, the SHIPOWNERS of Hydra and Spetses, who had financed the fleet and demanded control over finances. And running across all of them, the diaspora intellectuals and the Phanariots, who supplied constitutions and international legitimacy.

The first civil war, in 1824, pitted the constitutional government against Kolokotronis. The second, between late 1824 and early 1825, pitted the bloc of notables and islands against the Peloponnesian chiefs, who were defeated and imprisoned. The decisive detail is how it was financed: with the first installment of the 1824 London loan we examined in entrega 12. Money borrowed to make independence served instead to let the revolutionaries fight one another.

And the outcome came immediately: in February 1825, while the leadership was divided and disarmed, Ibrahim Pasha landed in the Peloponnese with the Egyptian army of Mehmet Ali, trained on European lines by French instructors. Within a year he had recovered nearly the entire peninsula. Kolokotronis had to be released from prison and restored to command. Missolonghi fell in April 1826 after a desperate sortie by the garrison; Athens fell in 1827. The revolution was militarily defeated.

The lesson worth drawing is not moralistic but analytical: insurgent movements do not split by default of virtue, but because they bring together coalitions with materially incompatible interests that the shared struggle keeps suspended and that the first inflow of resources detonates. The arrival of external money does not unify: it reopens the distributive dispute. Anyone who has watched the trajectory of Peruvian social coalitions after gaining access to resources — from regional fronts to trade associations — recognizes the pattern without needing examples.

sections.heading: Navarino: independence as someone else's decision
paragraphs: Greece did not win its independence on the battlefield. On October 20, 1827, in the Bay of Navarino, in the southwestern Peloponnese, the combined fleets of Great Britain, France, and Russia destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet within a few hours. By all accounts the battle was largely unpremeditated: the allied squadrons had entered the bay to apply pressure, an incident occurred, and the result was the annihilation of the Ottoman navy.

The reasons for the intervention were not philhellenic. Great Britain feared that Russia would act alone and win a protectorate over the Orthodox Greeks, with access to the Mediterranean. Russia wanted exactly that. France sought to recover Mediterranean standing. The solution the three agreed on was to create a small, weak Greek state, jointly supervised and guaranteed by all three, precisely so that none would control it alone. The London Protocols of 1830 and the treaty of 1832 fixed the borders: a line between the gulfs of Arta and Volos that left out Thessaly, Epirus, Macedonia, Crete, the eastern Aegean islands, and of course Constantinople. LESS THAN A THIRD OF THE GREEK POPULATION REMAINED WITHIN THE GREEK STATE.

That figure is the founding fact of the entire following century. A state that contains only a minority of its own nation cannot help but orient its foreign policy toward expansion, and from that will come the Megali Idea of the next entrega, and from that will come the catastrophe of 1922. The border of 1832 was not a mistake: it was a design for a balance of power among the great powers that took no account whatsoever of the resulting state's internal viability. It is the same procedure that later drew the borders of Africa and the Middle East, and by which Latin American border disputes were settled through external arbitration.

sections.heading: Kapodistrias: the attempt to build a state, and its failure
paragraphs: Ioannis Kapodistrias arrived as governor in January 1828, to a devastated country, its population decimated, its agriculture destroyed, and no institutions to speak of. He was, as we saw, a Corfiot and a former foreign minister to the tsar: the very choice signaled the tutelage.

His program was what any state-builder would have attempted: centralizing tax collection, creating a regular army in place of armed bands, founding schools, establishing a currency — the phoenix, the first modern Greek coin —, organizing a land registry, and distributing national lands confiscated from the Ottomans. And it collided head-on with the three real powers: the military chiefs, who did not want to disband their troops; the notables, who did not want to lose control of tax collection; and the shipowners, who did not want a state that would tax them. He governed in an increasingly authoritarian manner, suspended the assembly, and imprisoned opponents.

On October 9, 1831, he was assassinated at the door of a church in Nafplio by two members of the Mavromichalis clan of the Mani, whose chief he had imprisoned. It is hard to imagine a more exact symbol: the first head of state of modern Greece, trained in European imperial diplomacy, killed by a mountain family defending its clan autonomy against the law of the state. The entire tension between the modern state and local patrimonial power, on a single flight of steps.

The powers resolved the ensuing chaos by importing a king: Otto of Wittelsbach, second son of the king of Bavaria, seventeen years old, Catholic, who arrived in Nafplio in February 1833 with a Bavarian regency and Bavarian troops. That is the subject of the next entrega.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: 1821–1832 in Peru
paragraphs: The simultaneity with Peru is almost perfect, which is why it is worth reading them in parallel, year by year. While Greece bleeds itself in civil wars between 1824 and 1825, Peru fights Junín and Ayacucho in 1824 and consummates its independence. While Kapodistrias tries to build a state between 1828 and 1831, Peru goes through the war with Gran Colombia of 1828–1829 and the onset of caudillo instability. While the powers impose Otto in 1832, Peru enters the civil war that will lead to the Peru-Bolivia Confederation of 1836 and its destruction by Chile in 1839.

The two countries share, in that decade, exactly the same set of problems: no state apparatus, military chiefs with their own troops who recognize no civilian authority, unpayable foreign debt contracted before the state even existed, disputed borders, and an elite divided between incompatible projects. And they share, above all, the problem that Kapodistrias and Bolívar formulated in almost identical terms and with identical bitterness: how does one build legitimate authority where the only legitimacy available is that of the armed man?

It is the later divergence that matters. Greece received, along with tutelage, an imported state complete with bureaucracy, regular army, and external guarantee of its existence; the price was sovereignty. Peru retained more formal sovereignty and lacked a state apparatus for decades; the price was gamonalismo and fragmentation. There is no moral here about which path was better. There is a finding: both paths produce incomplete states, and both countries are still dealing with the particular form of incompleteness they inherited.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: who decides and who pays
paragraphs: Two contemporary resonances. The first is the memory of the revolution itself. The bicentennial of 2021 was a major state operation — the "Greece 2021" committee, exhibitions, restorations, the presence of foreign heads of state — and it also produced a serious historiographical debate in the Greek public sphere over the massacres, the civil wars, and external dependence, with angry reactions from nationalist quarters. It is exactly the kind of dispute Peru had at its own bicentennial in 2021, in the midst of an acute political crisis, in a country unable to agree on what it was celebrating. Round-number anniversaries do not produce consensus: they produce evidence that none exists.

The second is more structural. The pattern of 1827 — a country whose fate is decided in a negotiation among powers pursuing their own balance — has a perfectly recognizable contemporary version in the crisis of 2010–2015: the terms of the Greek bailout were set in meetings where the dominant interest was the stability of the European banking system and the containment of contagion risk, not Greece's recovery. The referendum of July 2015, in which 61 percent voted to reject the conditions, was followed within a week by the acceptance of harsher ones. We will return to this in Block V, but the parallel with 1832 should be planted here already: there are states whose formal sovereignty coexists with a structural conditionality that no election can reverse, and Greece has spent two hundred years as Europe's example of that condition. Peru has spent the same span as one of its American examples, with different instruments: not the tutelage of three guarantor powers, but the discipline of debt markets and credit-rating agencies.
